clinicalPearls: SCA15 is an autosomal dominant, purely cerebellar ataxia caused by heterozygous deletions or point mutations of ITPR1, the gene encoding the type 1 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor.
It is one of the most slowly progressive dominant ataxias, often evolving over decades with long-preserved mobility.
What was historically termed SCA16 is now recognised as the same ITPR1 disorder, and SCA29 is an allelic, congenital non-progressive ataxia.
Head and postural or action tremor (titubation) can be an early and prominent feature, sometimes preceding overt gait ataxia.
Whole-gene or partial ITPR1 deletions are a common mechanism, so copy-number analysis is essential and sequencing alone may miss the diagnosis.
MRI shows selective cerebellar atrophy, often most marked in the superior vermis, with sparing of the brainstem.
Age at onset spans childhood to late adulthood, and life expectancy is essentially normal.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA15 arises from heterozygous mutations of ITPR1 on chromosome 3p26, which encodes the type 1 inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor, a ligand-gated intracellular calcium-release channel of the endoplasmic reticulum that is very highly expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells. Partial or whole-gene deletions cause haploinsufficiency, while missense point mutations impair receptor function; both reduce inositol-trisphosphate-mediated calcium release and disturb Purkinje cell calcium signalling and synaptic plasticity, producing slow Purkinje cell dysfunction and degeneration. Allelic variation explains a phenotypic spectrum: heterozygous loss or point mutations give the adult SCA15 phenotype, other missense variants underlie the congenital non-progressive SCA29, and biallelic loss produces a severe infantile ataxic disorder.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 (CACNA1A) — slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia
SCA5 (SPTBN2), SCA11 (TTBK2) and SCA26 (EEF2) — dominant pure cerebellar ataxias
SCA29 (ITPR1) — allelic congenital non-progressive ataxia presenting in childhood
Essential tremor, when early head or action tremor dominates the picture
Sporadic late-onset cerebellar ataxia and the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy
additionalInvestigations: ITPR1 analysis that includes copy-number/deletion testing (such as MLPA or array comparative genomic hybridisation) as well as sequencing
Ataxia gene panel or exome with dedicated copy-number-variant calling
Exclusion of the common trinucleotide repeat-expansion ataxias
Brain MRI documenting vermian and hemispheric cerebellar atrophy
Family pedigree analysis and cascade testing with genetic counselling
Screen for treatable acquired causes before finalising a genetic diagnosis
redFlags: Congenital or very early-onset severe ataxia with developmental delay suggests an allelic (SCA29) or biallelic phenotype and different counselling.
Rapid progression, autonomic failure or early severe disability is atypical and suggests an alternative diagnosis such as multiple system atrophy.
Prominent extracerebellar features such as marked pyramidal, extrapyramidal or cognitive involvement warrant reconsideration.
reference.prognosis: SCA15 is very slowly progressive, with mobility often preserved for many years and a normal life expectancy; a minority progress to needing walking aids in later life.
pitfalls: Relying on sequencing alone and missing the common ITPR1 deletions that require copy-number testing.
Misdiagnosing early head or action tremor as essential tremor and overlooking the underlying ataxia.
Not recognising that historical SCA16 reports describe the same ITPR1 disorder.
Confusing the childhood-onset allelic form (SCA29) with an acquired or non-genetic cerebellar disorder.
management: Provide symptomatic and supportive care for this very slowly progressive, purely cerebellar ataxia, as no disease-modifying therapy for the ITPR1 defect exists
Treat prominent head and postural titubation and action tremor symptomatically
Maintain balance and gait with physiotherapy and mobility aids only as needed, given long-preserved mobility
Offer speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Reassure regarding the very slow progression and generally normal life expectancy, with periodic monitoring
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and cascade testing of relatives
